canonical_question: What specific failure mode or interface characteristic was observed when studying the adhesion of the film on 304 stainless-steel?

question_variants.question: What specific failure mode or interface characteristic was observed when studying the adhesion of the film on 304 stainless-steel?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The text mentions that the adhesion of the film on 304 stainless-steel was studied and that annealing improved adhesion and surface roughness. However, it does not specify the failure mode (e.g., adhesive vs. cohesive) or specific interface characteristics (e.g., delamination patterns, interfacial bonding strength values) observed during the adhesion study.

answers.answer: The study found that annealing at 300 °C improved the adhesion of the CuMoTaWV film to the 304 stainless-steel substrate and resulted in the lowest surface roughness. However, the text does not describe a specific failure mode or detailed interface characteristics observed during the adhesion testing.
answers.measurement_outcome: Improved adhesion, lowest surface roughness (2 nm Sa, 3 nm Sq).
answers.mechanism: Annealing improves surface roughness and adhesion.
answers.boundary_limitation: Specific failure mode or interface characteristics not described.
evidence_spans: The deposited high-entropy films were annealed at 300, 400, and 500 °C to increase the adhesion of the film to the 304 stainless-steel substrate.
The annealed CuMoTaWV film at 300 °C ( Figure 10 a) showed the lowest surface roughnesses of 2 nm (Sa) and 3 nm (Sq).

Based on these findings, the RHEA film annealed at 300 °C showed the lowest surface roughness ( Figure 10 d) and was thus chosen to study the tribological behavior and compared with the as-deposited film.

source_evidence_spans: The adhesion of the deposited film on the commercial 304 stainless-steel substrate was studied
